title: Adaptability and the Late-Modern Condition
author: Richard Claydon
summary: This companion essay steps back from the team rituals to ask why adaptability has become a precondition for leading at all. Claydon reads the question through five late-modern sociologists: Beck on the risk society, Giddens on the reflexive self, Sennett on the corrosion of character, Appadurai on global flows and Bauman on liquid modernity. He maps each of Maya's rituals onto one of these pressures, arguing that they are a practical response to the fractures of modern work. He holds that anchoring and agility are complements, since anchoring without agility becomes rigidity and agility without anchoring becomes drift. He criticises popular leadership frameworks for cherry-picking this sociology and trying to erase contradictions, and concludes that leadership is a provisional craft built on reflexivity, relationality and rhythm.
points: Beck's risk society means authority rests on preparedness rather than prediction, making regular clarity rituals a survival rhythm.
Sennett's critique shows that flexibility without relationship breeds precarity, which collaboration rituals with juniors counter by restoring voice and trust.
Traditional leadership ideals like steadfastness clash with Bauman's liquid modernity, so leaders need temporary moorings rather than fixed anchors.
Anchoring without agility becomes rigidity and agility without anchoring becomes drift, so ritual must bind the two.
Leadership programs fail when they try to erase contradictions rather than make them livable through reflexivity, relationality and rhythm.
quotes: It dissolves the fantasy of control. Strategy slides assume linear cause and effect; Beck’s world refuses both. In a risk society, authority no longer rests on prediction but on preparedness—the ability to move when the ground moves.
Leadership, in this light, is not a stable persona but a continual act of re-authoring. To lead is to make meaning in motion, to integrate new data without collapsing under it.
Flexibility promised freedom; it delivered fragmentation. Workers learned to reinvent themselves every few years, yet each reinvention eroded trust, memory, and belonging.

Traditional leadership ideals—steadfastness, authority, consistency—belong to the age of solids. Today’s leaders are judged by their ability to adapt, but that very adaptability corrodes the stability people crave.

Adaptability and anchoring are not opposites; they are complements. Anchoring without agility becomes rigidity; agility without anchoring becomes drift. The genius of ritual design is that it binds the two.

Most programs fail because they try to erase the contradictions these thinkers exposed. Maya’s rituals begin instead from acceptance: the contradictions are the work. Rituals don’t remove complexity; they make it livable.

What unites the late-modern sociologists is their rejection of certainty. Each describes a world where knowledge, identity, and structure are contingent. Leadership, therefore, cannot be mastery over that world; it must be craft within it.
